en: The Jātaka,
Great Section (Mahānipāta), Chapter on the Mūgapakkha (The Dumb and Paralysed)
1. The Mūgapakkha Jātaka:
"Do not display your wisdom;
be considered a fool by all living beings."
“Let all those people gather it;
in this way, your welfare will be secured.
“I shall do as you say.”
"Whatever you say to me, O deity,
you desire my welfare, mother;
you desire my benefit, O deity."
“Why indeed, charioteer, do you dig at the ground in such a hurry?
Being asked by me, my good man, explain.”
"What will you do with your coughing?
"To the king was born a son who is mute, one-sided, and senseless."
“I have been summoned by the king;
he has ordered me to bury his son in the forest.
“I am neither deaf nor mute,” [he said].
Neither partial nor deficient would a charioteer act unrighteously,
even if he were to bury you in the forest.
Behold my thighs and my arms,
and hear my words:
O charioteer, you would commit an unrighteous act!
“Are you a deity, or a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka Purindada, that you have buried me here in the forest?”
“Who are you, or whose son are you?
How shall we know you?
“I am neither a god nor a gandhabba.”
Nor am I Sakka Purindada;
I am the son of the King of Kāsi,
for whom you are being buried in the kāsu pit.
I am the son of that king upon whom you live as a dependent;
O charioteer, you would be acting unrighteously.
If you were to bury me in the forest under the shade of whichever tree you might sit or lie down beneath.
One should not break its branch,
for that evil person is a betrayer of friends;
as is the tree, so is the king.
As is the branch, so am I;
as is the person who has come into the shade, such are you, O charioteer.
A charioteer might act unrighteously by burying you in the forest;
yet he becomes one who has abundant food.
Even when he has gone abroad from his own home,
many depend upon him—
he who does not betray his friends.
To whatever country,
town, or capital city he goes,
everywhere he is honored.
He who does not betray his friends is not overcome by thieves,
nor is he despised by the kshatriyas.
He who does not deceive his friends overcomes all enemies; free from anger,
he returns to his home.
He is welcomed in the assembly;
he is the best among kinsmen—
he who does not deceive his friends.
Having honored others, one is honored;
being respectful, one becomes revered;
one comes to be sustained by praise and renown.
He who does not betray his friends,
being a worshiper, receives worship;
being one who pays homage, he receives homage in return.
One who does not betray friends attains fame and renown;
like a blazing fire, he shines forth.
He shines like a deity;
he is never deprived of glory—
he who does not deceive his friends.
Cattle are born to him,
and what is sown in his field grows;
he eats the fruit of what has been sown.
He who does not betray his friends—
such a person, even if fallen from a precipice, from a mountain, or from a tree, [is saved].
He who does not betray his friends finds a firm footing after he has passed away;
his continuity of being has deep roots.
Just as the wind cannot shake a banyan tree,
so enemies cannot overcome one who does not deceive his friends.
“Come, prince, I shall send you back to your own home;
rule the kingdom, O blessed one.”
"What will you do in the forest?
"Enough for me of that kingship,
or of kinsmen, or of wealth."
“If, O charioteer, my kingdom could be obtained through unrighteous conduct,
give me a bowl full of gains.”
"Prince, he has gone from here;
when you had departed, Prince, my father and mother gave [me away]."
The Orodhas, the Kumāras, the Vesiyānas, and the Brāhmaṇas— they too,
being well-pleased, gave gifts.
When the prince had gone,
the elephant-riders, the cavalrymen,
the charioteers, and the infantrymen—
With hearts full of joy,
they gave when you had departed, O prince;
the people of the countryside possess abundant grain.
“The guilds have assembled together;
let them give me gifts now that you,
O prince, have departed.”
“I have renounced father and mother,
and the kingdom and the town;
moreover, all princes— ”
I have no home of my own.
I was permitted by my mother and bestowed upon me by my father.
Having gone forth into homelessness in the forest,
one should not long for sensual pleasures,
even if others are not hurrying.
The fruit of my hope is being fulfilled;
I have matured the holy life—
know this, O charioteer.
Even for those who do not strive,
the goal of perfect practice ripens;
I am one whose holy life has reached its fruition.
“Having gone forth, you are free from fear on any side.
“Thus you speak with such pleasant discourse,
yet your speech is so harsh.”
"Why did he not speak then in the presence of his father and mother?
"It was not because I lacked connection or partiality," [he replied].
I am not deaf because of my lack of hearing;
I am not mute because of my lack of a tongue—
do not consider me to be mute.
I remember a former birth,
when I ruled as a king; having exercised sovereignty there—
I ruled there for twenty years in that terrible and most dreadful hell.
For eighty thousand years,
I was scorched in hell;
out of fear of that kingdom, I—
"Let them not consecrate me as king;
therefore, I did not speak then in the presence of my father and mother."
Having seated me on his lap,
my father instructed me in what is beneficial:
"Slay one, bind one."
One he shall have flogged with salt-corns;
one he shall impale upon a stake—
thus he instructs him.
Having heard those harsh words uttered by her,
though not deaf,
I appeared as if deaf.
Though not a partisan, I was considered a partisan;
I wallowed, completely submerged,
in my own urine and excrement.
Painful, limited, and joined with suffering—
this wretched life having come to pass,
One should act truthfully in every way.
Through the lack of wisdom and the failure to see the Dhamma, [one suffers].
Relying on this fragile life,
one might create enmity with someone;
even toward those who do not hasten [to harm].
The fruit of my hope is being fulfilled;
I have matured the holy life—
know this thus, O charioteer.
Even for those who do not hasten,
the true goal ripens;
I am one whose holy life has reached its fruition.
“Having gone forth, I am free from fear on all sides.
“I too shall go forth,
O prince, into your presence.”
“Summon me, venerable sir;
the going-forth appeals to me.
“Having had the chariot brought back, [he said:]”
Come, charioteer,
as one free from debt; for the going forth of one who is free from debt is praised by the seers.
“Since I did not do that very word which I spoke to you— may it be well with you—
you have done that very same word to me.”
Being thus entreated, you ought to do it.
Stay right here for now until I have brought the king.
“Perhaps your father, upon seeing you,
might be delighted and glad at heart.
“I shall do as you say.”
"O charioteer, as you have told me:
'I too wish to see my father who has come here.'"
"Come, my good man, turn back;
bring word of safety to your kinsmen—
to my mother and my father."
"Having been told this, you should offer your salutation.
Then, having grasped his feet and circumambulated him,
keeping him to the right;
The charioteer, having mounted the chariot,
arrived at the palace gate;
seeing the chariot empty, the mother—
She saw a single charioteer approaching;
with eyes full of tears,
she gazed at him while weeping.
“Here comes that charioteer,
having slain my own son;
surely my son has been killed.”
The one who increases the earth’s domain—
surely his enemies rejoice,
for surely his adversaries are filled with joy.
Seeing the charioteer who had returned after slaying my own son,
my mother saw the chariot empty.
Seeing a single charioteer approaching,
she, weeping with eyes full of tears, questioned him.
“Was he mute then, or was he lame?
Why did he lament as he was being struck down upon the ground?”
Tell me that, O charioteer:
how did the mute one avoid [using] his hands and feet?
"Being struck down by the earth,
tell me that when you are asked.
"I shall tell you, noble lady."
Grant me safety;
whatever I have heard or seen,
[I shall tell] in the presence of the prince.
“I grant you safety, my dear charioteer;
speak without fear whatever you have heard or seen.”
“In the presence of the prince.
“He is not mute, nor is he lame; he is one whose speech is fluent.”
Fearing indeed for his kingdom,
he committed many misdeeds in his dwelling;
he then recalled his former birth.
Where he exercised his sovereignty;
having exercised sovereignty there,
he fell into a terrible hell.
For twenty years he ruled there,
and for eighty thousand years—
He fell into hell.
Fearing for his kingdom, he thought,
"Let them not consecrate me to the kingship."
Therefore, in the presence of his father and mother, he did not speak then;
for he was endowed with all limbs and members.
Possessing height and circumference,
with speech that is expanded and wisdom,
he stands upon the path to heaven.
If you wish to see your own son, the prince,
come, and I will lead you there.
“Where Temiya finds peace.
“Harness the horses to the chariot;
bind the girths of the elephants.”
Let the conchs and drums resound;
let the single-toned instruments play.
Let the armored kettledrums sound forth.
Let the drums resound melodiously;
let the merchants follow me as I go to announce the birth of my son.
Let the Orodhas, the Kumāras,
the Vesiyāns, and the Brāhmaṇas quickly harness the carriages.
I went as one bringing news of my son.
Elephant-riders, cavalrymen,
chariot-warriors, and infantrymen—
"Quickly harness the vehicles;
I am going to inform my son.
The people of the countryside have gathered."
“The guilds have assembled;
quickly harness the carriages,
for I am going to announce the birth of my son.”
The charioteer, having harnessed the horses that draw swiftly,
approached the king’s gate.
“The horses are ready, O King.
“The fat ones fail in speed;
the thin ones fail in endurance.”
"Having avoided those that are too fat,
the horses have been harnessed in proper union.
Then the king, hurrying, [said:]
Having mounted his well-yoked chariot,
he addressed the women of the harem:
"All of you, follow after me."
With a yak-tail fan upon his head,
a sword, and a white parasol—
having mounted the chariot with these royal insignia—
Adorned with gold ornaments.
Then the king set forth,
placing the charioteer in front.
He quickly approached the place where Temiya was resting;
and seeing him coming, he—
Like the ocean with its splendor,
surrounded by a multitude of khattiyas,
Temiya spoke these words.
“Is it well, dear father?
Is it free from ailment, dear father?
And as for all the royal maidens...”
"My mothers are free from disease.
"May it be well with me, my son, and may you,
my son, be free from illness."
"And all the princesses are your mothers, free from disease.
"I hope, dear father, that you do not drink liquor?"
I hope you do not delight in liquor;
I hope your mind finds pleasure in truth, in the Dharma, and in generosity.
“I am a non-drinker of intoxicants, my son,
and moreover, liquor is not dear to me;
furthermore, in truth and in the Dhamma,”
“My mind delights in giving.
“I hope you are free from illness and fit for work;
I hope your draft animals are carrying their loads well?”
"I hope you have no ailments that afflict the body. "Indeed,
I am healthy and fit."
Moreover, my vehicle carries me along;
furthermore, I have no ailments that cause torment to the body.
“Is your border prosperous,
and is your center thick for you?
Are your storehouses and your treasury full?”
“Is it well-prepared for you?
“Furthermore, my ends are full,
and my middle is thick.”
"My storehouses and my treasury are all well-provided for.
"Welcome to you, Great King!"
Then they prepared a throne for his arrival,
upon which the king would sit.
Sit right here on this prepared mat of leaves;
taking water from this very place, [drink].
Wash your feet there.
This too is my leaf-stew,
king— without salt.
“Enjoy it, Great King;
I have come as a guest.
“I do not eat leafy greens.”
"This is not my food, O friend;
I eat rice-gruel with pure meat as a sauce."
“It seems marvelous to me,
even when I am alone in seclusion,
that they should eat such food as this.”
“By what does one’s complexion become serene?
“O King, I lie down alone upon a prepared bed of leaves.”
Because of that solitary dwelling of mine,
O King, my complexion has become serene;
nor do I have any fetters of craving.
Protection by the king is established;
through that comfortable sleep of mine,
O King, my complexion becomes serene.
I do not grieve for the past,
nor do I long for the future;
I maintain myself with what is present.
By that, one's complexion becomes serene.
Through yearning for the future and grieving for the past;
By this fools wither away,
like a green reed cut down.
"The elephant-force, the chariot-force..."
Horsemen, foot soldiers, and elephant-riders;
delightful dwellings,
my son, I give to you.
I give you even a harem of women,
adorned with every ornament;
my son, attend to them.
"You shall be our king.
We are skilled in dance and song,
trained women of the fourfold kind."
They will delight you with sensual pleasures;
what will you do in the forest?
Your daughters-in-law [will serve] you against rival kings.
I will bring them here adorned;
having given birth to sons by them,
you may then go forth into homelessness.
"You are young and youthful,
in the prime of your first bloom;
rule the kingdom, O Blessed One."
"What will you do in the forest?
"A youth should practice the holy life;
let one be a youth who practices the holy life."
For the going-forth of one who is young is praised by the seers;
a youth should lead the holy life.
One should be a youth practicing the holy life;
I shall practice the holy life,
for I have no need for kingship.
I see you, my dear child, a youth,
O mother and father,
my beloved son obtained with such hardship.
Without even reaching old age,
I see you dead— young,
a maiden of beautiful appearance.
Like a tender bamboo shoot that has been cut off,
life comes to its end; for even the young die.
Both men and women—
what person could place their trust therein,
thinking, "I am young in life"?
For one at the end of whose night life may become shorter,
like fish in a shallow pool of water—
What indeed is that childhood state?
The world is constantly assailed and constantly besieged.
“While the *amoghā* flowers are falling,
why do you anoint me to the kingdom?
“By what has the world been struck?”
And by what is it surrounded?
The bodies go forth not in vain;
tell me that when asked.
“The world is struck down by death,
surrounded by old age;
the nights pass away not in vain.”
Know this, O Kṣatriya:
just as when a loom is stretched out,
whatever is woven upon it;
Small is what must be crossed;
such is the life of mortals,
like a full torrent of water.
As one goes, one returns;
even so does the life of humans go,
as one goes, one returns.
Just as a full river carries away trees growing on its banks,
so too does old age and death carry away beings.
All living beings are swept away.
“The elephant corps, the chariot corps,
the cavalry, the infantry, and those clad in armor;”
"O son, I give you delightful dwellings;
I also give you a harem of women."
Adorned with all ornaments;
O son, attend to them,
for you shall be our king.
Skilled in dance and song,
these four women, well-trained,
will delight you in sensual pleasures.
"What will you do in the forest?
I shall bring you back a maiden,
adorned, from rival kings."
Having fathered sons upon them,
you may then go forth into homelessness later;
for you are still young and a youth.
"You are a youth who has only just attained his first maturity;
rule the kingdom, O Blessed One!
What will you do in the forest?"
Granaries and treasuries,
vehicles and armies,
and delightful dwellings—
"I give this to you, my son:
surrounded by a herd of cattle,
preceded by a throng of female slaves."
"Rule the kingdom, O Blessed One;
what will you do in the forest?
"What is the use of wealth that must eventually perish?"
Why die for the sake of a wife?
Why grieve over youth that is worn away, when one is overcome by old age?
In that state, what joy is there, what play,
what delight, or what quest for wealth?
What use have I for sons or wives?
O King, I am released from bondage,
for I understand thus:
"Death does not neglect me."
For one seized by the End-maker,
what joy is there, what seeking of wealth?
Like fruits that have ripened, [they must fall].
There is constant fear of falling;
likewise, for mortals who are born,
there is constant fear of death.
Some are not seen in the evening,
yet many people are seen in the morning;
some are not seen in the morning.
Many people were seen this evening.
One must perform one's duty today;
who knows if death will come tomorrow?
For we have made no compact with that Death who possesses a great army;
thieves merely covet wealth.
“O King, I am released from my bonds;
come, O King, turn back.
I have no need for kingship.”
The Mūgapakkha Jātaka is first.
